title: Building Closed-Loop Evals for a Multimodal Agent at Scale — Soumya Gupta & Jai Chopra, Uber
talk_summary: Uber Eats describes a multimodal image-enhancement agent pipeline with routing, editing, QA, and logging, and explains how they eval each stage against human-labeled golden data. They run production sampling, diagnosis, and config-only auto-tuning loops with guardrails and rollback, plus redundant QA gates and segment-level production metrics.

takeaways.technique: Flat structured run logging as eval substrate
takeaways.what_they_do: They log every agent step in one flat JSON so engineers and product can inspect individual cases and aggregate outcomes. They say logging must come first because otherwise there is nothing to optimize or learn from.
takeaways.evidence_quote: all of the agents in this end-to-end orchestration is within one It's It's basically a flat structure in this JSON.

takeaways.technique: Golden PR-defect set with recall guardrail
takeaways.what_they_do: They collect representative human-labeled examples with objective labeling guidelines, compare agent output to that golden set, and ship only if guardrail metrics are met. For routing, recall is the guardrail because bad cases must not slip through.
takeaways.evidence_quote: For routing, our guardrail metric is recall. We don't want any bad image to slip through our system.

takeaways.technique: Production sampling plus diagnoser auto-tuning loop
takeaways.what_they_do: They sample production data at a regular cadence, label it with the same human guidelines, compare agent output to labels, and use a diagnoser agent to localize the failing component. The diagnoser can write config and trigger auto-tuning, then benchmark against golden data before registering a new agent version with rollback.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Your diagnoser agent can write your config and trigger the auto-tuning pipeline here.

takeaways.what_they_do: They evaluate routers as classifiers with confusion matrices, and when routing to multiple branches/models they use an n-by-n matrix to measure whether each specific branch choice was correct.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of having a 2 by 2 matrix for your confusion matrix, you might actually have an n by n matrix.

takeaways.what_they_do: They keep multiple QA gates with some intentional redundancy to reduce the chance a failure reaches production. The final holistic gate also flags issues that upstream gates should have caught.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we think of this like a Swiss cheese model. So, we want to try and optimize for reducing the chance of a failure getting into production.

takeaways.what_they_do: They put a diagnoser above multiple feedback loops so it can ingest thumbs/freeform/production feedback, reflect on which agent or agents need optimization, and route the fix to the right configuration.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It can reflect on what actual agent within the overall system needs to be optimized
